KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong CAA will ramp up quickly behind backdoor
front dropping through the NC/VA border as of early Tue AM. 
Strong high pressure tempo wedges in from the north for today. 
This will briefly lock in a cooler and drier airmass with 
breezier conditions as gusts top out around 20-25 mph inland and
up to 40 mph for some coastal sections. Temperatures fall back 
to slightly below average with highs generally in the upper 
50s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Pattern quickly gets complex by mid-week as a 
potent sub-tropical jet will remain in place through the week. A
strong upper level trough will ride this jet eastward into the
Plains states. Finally, an upper low is forecast to deepen and 
dive southeastward out of the Canadian prairies and tracks 
towards the Ohio River Valley. The latter two features will 
undergo a complex interaction over the eastern CONUS, with the 
Plains trough digging further into the Gulf Coast and taking on 
a negative tilt as it interacts with the OH Valley low. We will
see a similar evolution at the mid- levels with two potent 
shortwave troughs.

This overall pattern favors surface cyclogenesis along the 
Southeastern coast, although how the aforementioned features 
interact will play a large role in the low's track and 
intensity. Some better tightening of 24/00Z guidance and
respective ensemble members in tracking the low over ENC vs
offshore. This trend leads to an inc in fcst winds from this
time yesterday. 

As the low tracks northward and deepens as it moves towards the
Carolinas, it will begin to buttress the surface high still 
wedged over the mid-Atlantic. The resulting pressure gradient 
will bring strong ENE winds to the region, peaking Wed night 
into the early morning hours on Thu, and most acutely felt over
the Outer Banks with gusts up to 50-55 mph Wed night. Gusts up 
to 40+ mph are also possible inland. This is a shift upwards 
from the previous forecast and would necessitate wind adv 
headlines for coastal locales. The higher winds also heightens 
concerns for coastal flooding...see KEY MESSAGE 3 for more 
details on this.

The low will also pull up a plume of very deep moisture from 
the Atlantic with PWATs forecast to exceed 2" (per climatology 
this is roughly 300%+ of normal for late November). With the 
strong ascent aloft, heavy rainfall is likely. The low track 
will determine the axis of heaviest rainfall. Some fine-tuning
of heavy rain axis with the best chances, 80-90+%, focused 
along the coastal counties. Hatteras Downeast Carteret through 
Hatteras island a probability of exceeding 4" at 40-50% (less 
than 20% farther inland). Even with the area in portions of 
severe to extreme drought, this level of rainfall could still 
pose a threat of flash flooding across the area especially in 
urban corridors. Latest RRFS and MPAS RRFSA are even more
concerning in fcsting even higher amounts than currently
advertised due to convective training embedded storms, and lead
to locally higher amts > 6". 

Speaking of thunder chances, still think the threat is slight
for all but the coastal areas, as weak instability will reside
inland. Closer to the coast, esp the OBX, will have to be
monitored for a localized svr threat, as strong cells over the
Gulf could approach the islands, esp Ocraoke and Hat island
which are closer to the warmer Gulf waters that lurk offshore
providing an iso tornado or waterspout threat overnight Wed. 
Have inc thunder chances to likely for the coastal waters 
generally south of C Hatteras. 

Low pres arrives Thur, and with it, a sharp reduction in winds
as they veer to the south and weaken to less than 20 mph as the
area becomes dry slotted. Have thus decreased precip quicker and
by Thur afternoon most of the showers should be shifting
offshore of the coast. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...ENC is currently experiencing the next round of
king tides this week with an increase in antecedant water 
levels. These are expected to peak through Thursday and then 
begin tapering off Friday and esp the weekend, and will be 
slightly higher than the cycle that occurred in October. Some 
minor water rises are possible today on the lower Pamlico sound
including the Neuse river with the northeast winds, as well as 
ocean- side locations along the Outer Banks just due to the
uptick in winds and the increasing tide levels.

Wednesday night is much more concerning as the approaching low
pres brings and even further inc in NE to E winds to gales
across the sounds and inland rivers (Pamlico and Neuse), and
brings the threat for impactful coastal flooding for these areas.
Most tidal locations across ENC are likely to see at least 
minor to moderate impacts, with the risk for major impacts for 
more typically vulnerable locations given forecast 
strengthening NE to E winds up the rivers. Interests should 
continue to closely monitor forecasts through the coming days.
